statement: A thirty-year-old agency’s booking site, redesigned for flights, hotels and tours, from a twelve-site benchmark to live pages.
team: Part-time product designer and strategist, with the agency’s team
heroCaption: The redesigned home page: one search box for flights, hotels, flight and hotel, and tours, above the agency’s offers.

snapshot.problem: Quick flight purchases and long, considered tours had to share one site, and the agency’s own judgement had to show next to the price.
snapshot.role: Product designer and strategist, part-time: the benchmark, the information architecture, the design language, every page of the booking site, the account area and a travel-planner concept.
snapshot.result: The redesigned booking site is live on tahagasht.com. The travel planner and the social layer are designed but are not on the site.

context.heading: A thirty-year-old agency with three kinds of trip
body: Taha Gasht is a Tehran travel agency that has sold trips for three decades: domestic and foreign flights, hotels in Iran and abroad, group tours with a Persian-speaking guide, and visas. Its website is the booking system for all of it, with a panel for partner agencies behind it.

Sina worked on it part-time as product designer and strategist. The Figma file states the brief on its cover: the changes to Taha Gasht’s main site. The work covered the public site from the first search to the traveller’s account, and a concept for what could come next.

problem.heading: A quick purchase and a long decision on one site
body: A domestic flight is bought in minutes, on price and time. A tour to Japan is weighed for weeks: the dates, the hotels, the documents, the guide and often a call with a consultant. The same site has to serve both.

The site also shares its flights and hotels with booking sites that sell them too. What an agency can add is judgement: which flight has a guaranteed seat, which hotel is well placed, which tour is worth the money. The redesign had to put that judgement next to the price.
problem.insight: A price list says what a trip costs. An agency can also say what to choose.

benchmark.heading: Twelve booking sites, captured side by side
body: Before drawing, Sina captured the full pages of twelve booking sites on the same day, next to Taha Gasht’s own: five Iranian sites that sell the same flights (Alibaba, Flytoday, MrBilit, Flightio and SafarMarket) and seven international ones (Booking.com, Expedia, Kayak, Skyscanner, Google Flights, Cheapflights and Wego).

Flight-booking app kits went into the same file as references for mobile flows, and later, for the social concept, the travel-experience pages of an Iranian booking site and Tripadvisor. None of that material is shown here: it is other people’s work.

ia.heading: The whole journey as a map before any screen
body: The first board maps the flight and hotel journeys module by module: the search page, the result list, the single flight or hotel, and the landing pages that search engines find. On the flight side, each module is tagged by where it comes from: Taha Gasht’s current structure, or a new idea.
Some new ideas are small, like buttons for the previous and next day, or a price calendar that marks public holidays. Others change what the site can do:
bullets: A price alert that can book the flight: the traveller saves passenger details and tops up the wallet by 20 to 30 percent over the fare, and the flight is booked when the price changes.
Sold-out flights stay in the list.
Hotels on a list and on a map share one filter, with the same results in both, and hovering a hotel in the list shows it on the map.
Reviews come from a third-party source at first, with the site’s own review system beside them.
Landing pages for routes and hotels show price trends once at least twelve months of data exist.
ia.insight: Every module has a source: kept from the current site, or a new idea.

suggestions.heading: Four ways to suggest a flight
body: Two opportunity trees ask what the agency can recommend. For flights there are four kinds of suggestion: the cheapest; charter flights, because on a charter the seat is guaranteed; the shortest, on foreign routes; and flights with special amenities for a limited time, set by hand in the back office.

The special-amenity branch is also where the agency can sell more: extra baggage, an upgrade to business, discounts on routes, a CIP lounge, a free hotel at a stopover. For hotels, the picks combine guaranteed rooms, access to the city centre and price. A second board maps the tour page the same way, starting with Japan.
suggestions.insight: The agency’s pick became a sort tab on the result list, next to cheapest and best.

language.heading: Three rounds on one card
body: The flight ticket card carries most of the site. It repeats down every result list, opens into flight, price and refund details, and sets the pattern for hotel and tour cards. So the design language was worked out on it, in three rounds: a first iteration, a third version of the ticket, and final versions that compare shadows, card backgrounds and borders on the same grey page.
The type is Yekan Bakh, set for Persian throughout. Earlier sketches in the file try two price calendars, one for domestic and one for foreign flights, and a ticket that opens in place.

flights.heading: Flights: choose by price, by time or by the agency’s pick
body: Flight results open with a strip of dates and their lowest fares, so a cheaper day is visible before any scrolling. Three sort tabs sit above the list, cheapest, best and Taha Gasht’s pick, and each shows its price and total time.

The filters follow what matters on these routes: a charter or systemic ticket, the number of stops, whether a stopover needs a visa, the cabin and the baggage. Every card shows the seats left and opens a window with the flight’s details, the price for adults, children and infants, and the refund rules, which list penalties and sales restrictions. A price alert sits in the list.
The search box handles one-way, round-trip and multi-city trips, and the flight version of the home page adds a table of last-minute charters.
flights.insight: A stopover visa gets its own filter: a cheap connection through Europe needs a Schengen visa.

hotels.heading: Hotels: where it is and what guests said
body: Hotel results come as a list or on a map, with one set of filters for both: price range, stars, the type of stay (hotel, boutique hotel or hostel) and the city’s districts. A card carries the price per night, the stars and, where it applies, the agency’s pick.

The hotel page breaks the rating into staff, location and cleanliness, lists nearby sights with the time to reach them on foot, by car or by metro, and lets guests add a review with photos. Rooms are compared on the same page, with a request for extra services before booking.
hotels.insight: Distances are given in minutes and by mode, the way a traveller plans a day.

tours.heading: Tours: a decision made with a person
body: Tours are where the agency is strongest, and where a purchase takes longest. The tour list filters by what a traveller wants from the trip: the season or holiday, such as Nowruz or Christmas, the weather, the aim (rest or adventure) and the kind of activity, from nature and history to festivals, food and shopping.

A tour page, drawn first for Japan, answers the questions a consultant usually hears: the packages and their dates, the price by hotel and room with children’s rates, a calculator for the whole group, the plan for each day, the hotels, the services included (a Persian-speaking guide, the visa, insurance, the CIP lounge at Tehran’s airport) and the documents needed. A call-back form, a phone number and WhatsApp stay close throughout.
The page also shows the agency’s record, its years in business, its passengers and their satisfaction, which the tour board had planned as competitive advantages.
tours.insight: A tour is still sold by a consultant. The page prepares the traveller for that call.

home.heading: A home page for three kinds of trip
body: The home page opens with one search box and four tabs: hotel, flight, flight and hotel, and tour. Below it, rows change with the season and the traveller: recently viewed trips, a row of trips to the south, last-minute flights and suggested hotels. The page also comes in a version for each product: flights, hotels, flight and hotel, and tours.

Further down, the page makes the case for the agency: its features, how to buy a ticket, passengers’ reviews, a call-back form with the hours it is answered, and a first invitation to the travel planner: “Build your own adventure.” On phones, four full-screen stories introduce the Travel Maker, one step each.

account.heading: Checkout and the traveller’s account
body: Checkout runs in five steps, shown across the top: choose a ticket, enter the passengers, confirm the details, pay, and issue the ticket. Saved passengers can be picked from a list, and new ones are added with their passport details beside a summary of the flight.

After the purchase, the account has eight sections: travels, passengers, wallet, bookmarks, profile, messages, support and sign-out, most drawn with their dialogs and empty states. Travels shows each ticket’s status, opens the e-ticket, tracks the flight and starts a refund by route and passenger. The wallet, called the Taha card, is topped up by a set or a custom amount and pays out to a bank account. Support works as tickets, each with its own thread of replies.
Sign-in works with a password or a one-time code, and a help centre gathers the questions, the buying guide and support.

next.heading: What could come next: plan a trip, then share it
body: With the booking site drawn, Sina designed a concept to bring travellers back between trips. The Travel Maker plans a trip in four steps: the plan itself, with the route, the dates, the transport and the stay; the fellow travellers, with their names and phone numbers; the activities, day by day; and how to publish the trip. Activities come as types, such as historic sites, food, shopping, rest or local events, each placed on a map with photos or documents, and new days can be added.

The social layer lets travellers post a tour with its price per person, dates and departure city, share experiences rated on satisfaction, value for money and whether they would recommend the place, and write travelogues that link to a tour or a hotel.

A strategy board came with it. It sets seven goals, from sales and personalised offers to loyalty and brand awareness; eight drivers that would bring people back, from points and badges to referrals; and the risks beside them: slow early engagement, cost and a slow return, moderating content, privacy and negative feedback. A system map places each format (blog, interactive map, post, Reels and travelogue) where travellers would meet it: the feed, explore, the home page, campaigns and inside tour pages.
next.insight: The strategy board lists the risks beside the goals.

shipped.heading: Live on tahagasht.com
body: The redesign was built, and it is live on tahagasht.com. The live pages follow the maps. Flight results carry the charter or systemic label and buttons for the previous and next day. The Japan tour page opens with the agency’s record, three decades, 99 percent passenger satisfaction and more than 6,500 travellers, and keeps its consultation blocks and tabs for documents, prices, the best time to travel, cities and sights.
The Travel Maker and the social layer are not on the live site. They remain a designed next step.

decisions.heading: Five decisions behind the site
decisions.lede: The boards and the pages make these choices visible.

items.title: Show the agency’s pick next to cheapest and best
items.why: Any booking site can sort by price. Taha Gasht can also say which flight it would choose. As a sort tab, that judgement sits where the traveller chooses, and each tab shows its price and time so the trade-off is plain.
items.alternatives: One price sort, or a badge on a few cards.
items.tradeoff: The pick has to be kept up by people: the board marks special-amenity flights as set by an admin or a manager.
items.evidence: The Ticket and Hotel opportunity trees; the sort tabs on the result list.

items.title: Make charter and systemic a label and a filter
items.why: On a charter the seat is guaranteed, which is why the opportunity tree suggests it. The difference changes what the traveller is buying, so it sits on every card and in the filters.
items.tradeoff: One more label on a card that already carries times, stops and seats.
items.evidence: The live result list shows the label on every card.

items.title: A price alert that can book the flight
items.why: Seats on crowded routes sell out and fares change. A traveller who saves passenger details and tops up the wallet with a margin can have the flight booked when the price moves, without watching the site.
items.alternatives: An alert that only sends a message.
items.tradeoff: The traveller keeps 20 to 30 percent over the fare in the wallet.
items.evidence: The information architecture’s price-notification branch, and the alert on the result list.

items.title: Sell tours through a conversation
items.why: A group tour is a long decision, with documents and visas. The tour page answers the common questions, costs the whole group with a calculator, and keeps a call-back form and a phone number close, so the consultant’s call starts further along.
items.alternatives: Instant checkout for tours, as for flights.
items.tradeoff: The site hands the sale to people, so its pace is the sales team’s.
items.evidence: The tour page’s call, buy and notify states; the consultation blocks on the live Japan tour page.

items.title: One filter for the list and the map
items.why: A hotel’s value depends on where it is. One set of filters, the same results in both views and a hover that links them let a traveller switch views without losing their place.
items.tradeoff: Both views must load the same results, the map included.
items.evidence: The information architecture board: filters synced between the list view and the map, with the same result for both.

items.title: Write down how a flight earns the agency’s pick
items.body: Taha Gasht’s pick is the most distinctive idea on the result list, and the file never says how a flight earns it. A short rule, agreed with the sales team, would keep the tab honest and give travellers a reason to trust it.

items.title: Test the tour page with travellers
items.body: The tour page answers the questions consultants hear, but the file holds no test with travellers. A few sessions with people planning a trip would show which answers they look for first, and which they still pick up the phone for.

items.title: Start the social layer with one format
items.body: The concept covers posts, Reels, travelogues, a map and a planner at once. Starting with one format, travelogues linked to a booked tour, would have shown whether travellers post at all before the rest was built.
